title: Overview
description: A small Go CLI, Caddy routing, and one directory for every local app.
text:
Watch the demo  → Read the quickstart 
 A NAME FOR EVERY LOCAL APP app.test → Caddy → localhost:3000 Unregistered local name? Open the app directory. 
 Keep the port. Give it a name. 
 Localproxy is a Go CLI that generates and reloads Caddy routes. Register a name yourself, load names from a project file, or discover listening HTTP apps and give them random names. The directory keeps the registered domain and original localhost address together. 
 # proxy.yaml
app: 3000
api: 8080 
 These register  app.test  and  api.test . Browser URLs also need local DNS and certificate trust, and HTTPS depends on the  client’s wildcard compatibility . The reserved name  home.test  opens the directory. A configurable suffix lets you use names such as  app.dev.test . 
 Start with the isolated demo: it uses temporary files and high ports, and needs no DNS changes or system certificate installation. The  TLS compatibility note  explains why its HTTPS walkthrough uses  .dev.test . 
 Build your local workflow 
 01 / CONFIGURE Names as project data ↗ YAML or JSON defaults, with persistent CLI and browser overrides. 02 / DISCOVER An editable directory ↗ Search, copy an address, rename with confirmation, and undo. 03 / CONNECT See your Tailscale URLs ↗ Existing hostname and IP links, with availability made explicit. 04 / VERIFY Inspect the evidence ↗ Real screenshots, repeatable examples, tests, and an independent review. 
 A directory you can work from 
 Real app capture from an isolated fixture using the default .test suffix. Ports are assigned at startup. 
 See a name change, end to end 
 This recording uses the real directory with two running demo apps. Watch a search, edit, confirmation, successful rename, and Undo. The localhost port stays the same throughout. 
 
 
 
 
 Your browser cannot play this video.  Download the MP4 demo . 
 Real browser recording from an isolated local fixture. No audio; captions describe the actions.  Download MP4  ·  Editing guide 
 Read the demo walkthrough The directory shows api.test and app.test, each with its original localhost URL. Searching for api filters the directory to the matching app. Clear the search, edit app.test, and enter storefront. Save opens a confirmation showing app.test becoming storefront.test. Confirm the rename. The new domain appears with the original port, and the success message offers Undo. Undo restores app.test. The recording script verifies both name changes through real Caddy requests. 
 Use the same names in your tools 
 localproxy add app 3000
localproxy lookup http://localhost:3000
# app.test
localproxy lookup 3000 --json
localproxy config export --format yaml 
 Use JSON or YAML in scripts, export the full configuration, and install  CLI guidance for coding agents . Names from project files remain defaults until you override them. 
 What runs where 
 Caddy handles application traffic. The Go CLI manages the registry and configuration; an optional Go HTTP server provides the editable directory. Generated app listeners bind to loopback. Tailscale integration displays existing access paths and does not expose localhost apps. 
 The current implementation is Linux-oriented: discovery uses  ss , registry locking uses Unix file locks, and the machine setup script targets Arch/Omarchy. It is a source project with reproducible local checks, not a packaged cross-platform installer. 

 These documentation pages and demo media are public. The application source repository is currently private; building and running the CLI requires repository access. The  quickstart  documents the workflow for people with access.

title: Quickstart
description: Run a complete, isolated demo before changing your machine.
text:
1. Build the CLI 
 Use Linux, Go 1.24 or newer, Python 3.10 or newer, curl, and a Caddy executable. Caddy 2.11.4 is the version tested for this project. Install Caddy using its  official installation guide ; place the executable at  bin/caddy , on PATH, or set  CADDY_BIN . 
 git clone https://github.com/aaronS7/local-proxy.git
cd local-proxy
go build -o bin/localproxy . 
 The repository is private; cloning requires GitHub access. Run the following commands from the repository root. 
 2. Run the isolated demo 
 python3 scripts/docs-demo.py \
  --suffix dev.test \
  --state-file .local/docs-demo.json 
 Keep this terminal open. The script launches two small HTTP apps, Caddy, and the editor. It chooses unused high ports, creates a temporary registry and project map, and prints a directory URL you can open directly. Press Ctrl+C to stop the processes and remove temporary files. 
 Open the printed  directory_url . You will see  app.dev.test  and  api.dev.test , their localhost ports, and their editing controls. Domain links require local DNS; the direct directory URL works immediately. 
 The demo uses  .dev.test  so strict OpenSSL clients can validate its wildcard certificate. The application default remains  .test . See  certificate compatibility . 
 3. Send a request through Caddy 
 In another terminal, read the dynamically assigned ports.  --resolve  directs only this curl request to loopback; it does not change your machine’s resolver. 
 HTTP_PORT=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open(".local/docs-demo.json"))["ports"]["http"])')
HTTPS_PORT=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open(".local/docs-demo.json"))["ports"]["https"])')
CA_FILE=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open(".local/docs-demo.json"))["ca_file"])')

curl --noproxy '*' --fail \
  --resolve "app.dev.test:$HTTP_PORT:127.0.0.1" \
  "http://app.dev.test:$HTTP_PORT/"

curl --noproxy '*' --fail --cacert "$CA_FILE" \
  --resolve "app.dev.test:$HTTPS_PORT:127.0.0.1" \
  "https://app.dev.test:$HTTPS_PORT/" 
 Both requests reach the app fixture. The second verifies the certificate chain and hostname against the demo’s CA. There is no  --insecure  step. 
 4. Make the name yours 
 In the directory, choose  Edit  next to  app.dev.test , enter  studio , choose  Save , then confirm. The port stays the same. Use  Undo  to restore the previous name. 
 You can also rename from the CLI. Run these before the browser rename, or undo it first: 
 REGISTRY=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open(".local/docs-demo.json"))["registry"])')
./bin/localproxy -config "$REGISTRY" rename app studio
./bin/localproxy -config "$REGISTRY" reload
./bin/localproxy -config "$REGISTRY" list 
 The listing keeps  studio.dev.test  after reload even though the project map still calls that port  app . CLI and UI edits persist as overrides. 
 5. Verify the whole example 
 python3 scripts/verify-docs-example.py 
 The verifier starts its own demo, checks real proxy responses and HTTPS, exercises project files and edits, and tears down its temporary services. Read  Verification  for the exact scope and evidence. 
 Next, set up a  project map  for your own apps and configure  DNS and HTTPS  for normal browser URLs.

title: Configuration
description: Project defaults, persistent overrides, and predictable precedence.
text:
A project map 
 Put a flat name-to-port map in  proxy.yaml : 
 app: 3000
api: 8080 
 Or use  proxy.json : 
 {
  "app": 3000,
  "api": 8080
} 
 Short names gain the configured suffix. Full names under that suffix also work. Ports must be integers and each port must have one name in the map. Use  {}  for an empty map. Keep one format in a directory; if both exist, select one explicitly on each CLI command that reads the map. 
 ./bin/localproxy -file proxy.yaml generate
./bin/localproxy -file proxy.json generate 
 Naming precedence 
 Priority Name source How it changes 1 CLI / UI override add ,  rename , or browser edit 2 Project file Edit the map and run  reload 3 Discovery Random name when a new HTTP port is found 
 ./bin/localproxy rename app studio
./bin/localproxy reload
# studio.test keeps its name, even if the map still says app. 
 The project map is never rewritten.  remove  records a suppressed port, so discovery and the map do not immediately restore it. Use  add <name> <port>  to restore it. Deleting a map entry removes that file-managed route on reload, while overrides and unrelated discovered routes remain. 
 There is no reset-override command yet. To return a route to its file default, stop concurrent writers, remove that route’s  name_source: "override"  field in the registry, and reload. 
 Which file gets read? 
 An explicit  -file  path, when given. A map in the current working directory. The remembered absolute project-file path. A map next to the registry. 
 A missing remembered file or invalid map causes an error. Files are not watched. The UI reads the map on requests, so it can display an edited default before Caddy has applied it; run  reload  after changing the file. 
 The persistent registry 
 routes.json  stores proxy settings, registrations, name sources, and the selected project file. Use  -config  before the command to select a different registry. This example uses high ports and enables the editor backend: 
 {
  "suffix": "dev.test",
  "http_port": 18081,
  "https_port": 18443,
  "admin_port": 2021,
  "directory_address": "127.0.0.1:18083",
  "tailnet": false,
  "routes": [
    {"domain": "app.dev.test", "port": 3000}
  ]
} 
 Reserve distinct, available HTTP, HTTPS, admin, and editor ports. App ports cannot use those ports. Upstreams must accept connections at  127.0.0.1:<port> . The suffix can contain several labels, but each app gets exactly one label before it:  app.dev.test  works for suffix  dev.test ;  branch.app.dev.test  does not. 
 To inspect or save this registry after applying project-map precedence, run  localproxy config export  (JSON on stdout), or  localproxy config export -o snapshot.yaml  (YAML file). See  configuration export  for format flags, file handling, and portability details. 
 Apps with Host checks 
 By default, Caddy preserves the incoming hostname. If an app only accepts localhost, add  "localhost_host": true  to its registry route and reload. Caddy then sends  Host: localhost:<port> . Renaming preserves this setting. 
 CLI writes and Caddy reloads are separate steps. A failed CLI reload can leave the new registry saved while old routes still run. Fix the reported problem and retry  reload . See the  code review .

title: Discovery & editing
description: Discover HTTP services, find their addresses, and edit names in the browser.
text:
Find listening HTTP apps 
 ./bin/localproxy discover
./bin/localproxy list
./bin/localproxy rename curious-otter studio 
 The last command is illustrative: replace  curious-otter  with a name from your actual listing. Discovery inspects TCP listeners with  ss  and probes IPv4 localhost with HTTP HEAD. Any valid HTTP response qualifies, including 401, 404, or a redirect. Redirects are not followed. 
 It skips ports below 1024, its proxy/admin/editor ports, and already registered or suppressed ports. Probes use a two-second timeout and up to eight concurrent requests. HTTPS-only and IPv6-only upstreams are not discovered. This is a manual scan; stopped apps are not automatically removed. 
 Enable the editor 
 Set  directory_address  in the registry to  127.0.0.1:18083 , then start the backend in a separate terminal: 
 ./bin/localproxy -config /absolute/path/routes.json ui \
  --listen 127.0.0.1:18083 
 Reload a running proxy with the same registry, or start it: 
 ./bin/localproxy -config /absolute/path/routes.json reload
# If Caddy is stopped, use start instead of reload. 
 The UI process must remain running. Without  directory_address , generated Caddy pages provide a static directory with no edit controls. The editor itself accepts loopback listeners only. 
 Edit, confirm, undo 
 Watch the recorded workflow , including a real rename and Undo. 
 Search by name or port. Press  /  to focus search. Choose  Edit  and enter the new name. Choose  Save  or press Enter to review the old and new domains. Confirm  Rename app . Use  Undo  in the success message if needed. 
 Escape cancels an edit. Invalid, duplicate, and reserved names are rejected. A revision token prevents stale browser edits from overwriting a newer change. If a conflict occurs, refresh and try again. 
 Enter a short name; the domain suffix and original localhost port stay visible. 
 The confirmation previews the name change before submitting it. Capture uses the default .test suffix. 
 A successful browser rename applies Caddy routes before reporting success and persists the override. The UI attempts rollback if later file persistence fails. Ambiguous network failures and rollback failures still need operator attention; this is not a multi-system transaction guarantee. 
 What the fallback means 
 Registered app requests go to their original localhost ports. Their own 404 responses remain 404s. A registered app that stops returns an upstream error; the directory is a list of registrations, not a health monitor. 
 Unregistered names under the configured suffix and the reserved  home  name open the directory, including deep paths. In editable mode, the Host check allows localhost, configured single-label local names, and this machine’s known Tailscale addresses. An unrelated hostname receives 403. The static fallback has no equivalent Host check. 
 DNS must first send the request to this proxy. A fallback cannot intercept arbitrary domains on the Internet. HTTPS also needs a certificate the client accepts for the requested hostname. 
 On a smaller screen 
 The same directory becomes stacked cards on mobile. 
 A custom Caddy instance 
 ./bin/localproxy -config /absolute/path/routes.json ui \
  --listen 127.0.0.1:18083 \
  --proxy-admin 127.0.0.1:2022 \
  --proxy-config /absolute/path/instance/caddy.json 
 Use this when the running Caddy instance has a different admin endpoint or config path. UI edits preserve custom listeners and a separate directory server. Ordinary CLI reloads regenerate the standard servers; do not assume they preserve hand-edited Caddy configuration.

title: Tailscale links
description: Hostname first. IP second. Existing access stays in your control.
text:
Enable link discovery 
 ./bin/localproxy discover --tailnet
# Or, for an already running instance:
./bin/localproxy reload --tailnet

# Disable and persist that preference:
./bin/localproxy reload --tailnet=false 
 The flag adds  Tailnet hostname  followed by  Tailnet IP . It reads this machine’s Tailscale status, existing Serve configuration, and listening ports. Hostnames come from Tailscale status; see  Tailscale’s MagicDNS documentation  for name resolution. 
 Enable the setting with  discover ,  generate ,  start , or  reload  before starting the UI. The current  ui --tailnet  invocation accepts the flag but does not apply it. 
 How URLs are chosen 
 Column URL selection Hostname An existing Tailscale Serve root proxy for this app, when found; otherwise the machine’s hostname at the original HTTP port. IP The Tailscale IPv4 address at the original HTTP port, with IPv6 as fallback. 
 An existing Serve HTTPS URL keeps its certified hostname. The IP column remains an HTTP URL at the original port, avoiding a hostname certificate mismatch on an IP address. Direct links without a detected matching listener appear as unavailable text. Firewall rules and tailnet access policies still determine whether detected listeners can be reached. 
 Display does not create access 
 --tailnet  does not change an app’s bind address, create a Serve entry, enable Funnel, or expose the local proxy. An app listening only at  127.0.0.1  remains local to this machine. An app must already have a suitable listener or Serve route for its displayed link to work remotely. 
 The demo and screenshots keep tailnet discovery disabled for portability. They do not claim to verify another machine’s Tailscale access. 
 Reach the directory remotely 
 Serving the directory to your tailnet is a separate setup step. The Go UI must bind to loopback. Use a dedicated Caddy server listening on the machine’s Tailscale IP whose only route proxies to that UI. Keep app routing on its original loopback listeners. 
 For example, the directory-only server object in an instance-specific Caddy JSON config looks like this. Replace the example IP with your own Tailscale address and choose an available port: 
 {
  "listen": ["100.101.102.103:18082"],
  "routes": [{
    "handle": [{
      "handler": "reverse_proxy",
      "upstreams": [{"dial": "127.0.0.1:18083"}]
    }]
  }],
  "automatic_https": {"disable": true}
} 
 This is a server object to merge under  apps.http.servers , not a complete configuration or a CLI flag. Use  custom instance options  to preserve it during browser edits. Full CLI regeneration can replace manual additions. The directory-only route makes arbitrary paths reach the editor instead of app upstreams. 
 Anyone allowed to reach this editable directory can rename apps. It has same-origin, Host, CSRF, and revision checks, but no separate user account system. Use your tailnet’s access controls to define who can reach it. 
 Refresh behavior 
 The static page refreshes its tailnet information when generated. The editable UI caches Tailscale lookups for 15 seconds and refreshes them on requests. A disconnected or unavailable daemon produces an explanatory status; local directory links remain available.

title: DNS & HTTPS
description: Understand name resolution, certificate trust, and machine setup.
text:
Choose a local suffix 
 Localhost is not the only name you can use. Localproxy defaults to  .test , which is reserved for testing by  RFC 2606 . A suffix such as  dev.test  works too. Set the registry’s  suffix  before creating routes, and configure your resolver for that suffix. 
 The reserved directory name is  home.<suffix> . App names have one label before the suffix. The generated certificate covers that suffix and its wildcard. 
 Certificate compatibility 
 Current limitation: the default  *.test  certificate passes this project’s Go TLS tests, but curl/Python clients using OpenSSL reject it for  app.test  because of their wildcard hostname rules. Trusting the CA does not fix a hostname mismatch. 
 The isolated HTTPS example uses suffix  dev.test  and certificate  *.dev.test , which the verifier checks with hostname and chain verification enabled. This is a workaround using existing configuration, not an application fix. Browser compatibility should be tested in the actual browser and trust store you use; HTTP screenshots do not verify HTTPS behavior. 
 Test without installing anything 
 The  quickstart  uses curl’s  --resolve  and  --cacert . These choose a loopback address and CA for one command, without changing DNS or system trust. Use this path to separate routing failures from machine setup problems. 
 Arch / Omarchy setup 
 The included setup script targets Arch/Omarchy with systemd-resolved and the default  .test  suffix. It installs a dedicated dnsmasq service, routes  ~test  lookups to it, trusts this instance’s CA, and gives  bin/caddy  permission to bind ports 80 and 443. It is not a generic Linux or macOS installer. 
 For a registry using the default suffix and ports, first generate the config and provision the CA via Caddy validation: 
 ./bin/localproxy generate
./bin/caddy validate --config .local/caddy.json
sudo bash scripts/install-system.sh "$PWD" 
 Read  the script  before running it. It expects the local CA root file to exist. It starts Caddy directly unless an existing localproxy user service is present. Its final curl HTTPS check can hit the default-suffix compatibility issue described above; the machine changes occur before that check. 
 The script is written for  .test  and its verification URL is  home.test . With a different suffix, configure and verify your resolver separately. DNS-over-HTTPS in the browser may need an exception for local names. Browser-specific certificate stores may need the root imported separately. 
 Keep local trust local 
 Generated CA data lives at  .local/caddy-data  beside the registry. The public root is  pki/authorities/local/root.crt  beneath that directory. The directory also holds the CA’s private key and should remain private and untracked. 
 After replacing  bin/caddy , reapply any file capability needed for privileged ports. Generated listeners bind to IPv4 and IPv6 loopback; upstream connections use IPv4 loopback. 
 Stop and remove setup 
 Use  localproxy stop  for a manually started instance. If a user service manages it, use  systemctl --user disable --now localproxy.service  so its restart policy does not bring it back. The  repository removal guide  lists DNS, trust, and capability cleanup.

title: CLI reference
description: Commands, flags, and the files they read and write.
text:
Invocation 
 localproxy [-config routes.json] [-file proxy.yaml|proxy.json] [--tailnet] <command> 
 Examples use  ./bin/localproxy  when running from a source checkout.  -config  and  -file  go before the command.  --tailnet  is normalized so it can appear before or after a command; use  --tailnet=false  to disable it. 
 Commands 
 Command Effect 
 add <name> <port> Register or update a manual name; replace another name for that port and clear its suppression. 
 rename <old> <new> Persist an override for an existing route without changing its port. 
 remove <name> Remove the registration and suppress its port from maps and discovery. 
 discover Scan listening HTTP ports and persist random names for new apps. 
 lookup <port|localhost-url> Print the registered domain for a localhost port. Supports text, JSON and YAML. 
 list Print merged names and localhost URLs, or a JSON/YAML array. Does not probe app health or apply routes. 
 config [export] Export the full merged Local Proxy configuration as JSON or YAML, to stdout or a file. 
 generate Read the project map, save the registry, and write Caddy JSON. Does not start or reload Caddy. 
 start Generate configuration and start Caddy in the background. 
 run Generate configuration and run Caddy in the foreground. 
 reload Re-read project defaults, generate configuration, and ask the configured Caddy admin endpoint to load it. 
 stop Stop Caddy through the registry’s admin endpoint. 
 trust Invoke Caddy’s trust command for this instance’s local CA; may require system permission. 
 ui Run the editable directory backend. Does not start Caddy. 
 agents [print | install] Print bundled CLI instructions, or preview and confirm a managed section in AGENTS.md. No registry or Caddy access. 
 skill [print | install] Print the Local Proxy skill, or preview and confirm installation of SKILL.md. No registry or Caddy access. 
 
 Route mutations regenerate configuration and reload when the configured admin endpoint responds. CLI reload failures can leave saved changes unapplied; see  the failure mode . 
 Lookup and machine-readable output 
 ./bin/localproxy lookup 3000
./bin/localproxy lookup http://localhost:3000/path
./bin/localproxy lookup localhost:3000 --json
./bin/localproxy lookup 'http://[::1]:3000' --format yaml
./bin/localproxy list --json 
 Default lookup output is one domain and a newline, for example  app.test . HTTP(S) URLs must use  localhost  or a loopback IP. A URL without an explicit port uses 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS. Paths, queries and fragments are ignored. Credentials, remote hosts, unsupported schemes and invalid ports are rejected. Lookup does not resolve DNS or contact the app. 
 Both  lookup  and  list  accept  --format text|json|yaml ,  --json , or  --yaml . Choose one format flag; it can appear before or after the lookup input. Global  -config  and  -file  still go before the command. 
 Example JSON for an app registered on port 3000: 
 {
  "domain": "app.test",
  "port": 3000,
  "localhost_url": "http://localhost:3000",
  "http_url": "http://app.test",
  "https_url": "https://app.test",
  "name_source": "override"
} 
 Lookup produces one object. List produces an array sorted by domain, including  []  when there are no routes. YAML has the same fields and types as JSON. Proxy URLs include the registry's non-default HTTP and HTTPS listener ports; the lookup's plain domain output never includes a port.  name_source  is  override ,  file ,  discovered , or an empty string for an unlabeled legacy entry. 
 domain=$(./bin/localproxy lookup 3000)
./bin/localproxy lookup 3000 --json | jq -r '.https_url'
./bin/localproxy list --json | jq -r '.[].domain' 
 Both queries read the same merged configuration, including project defaults, manual overrides and suppressed ports. They do not write files, start Caddy or prove that saved routes are running. Missing matches, multiple domains on one port, invalid options and configuration errors exit with status 1, diagnostics on stderr and empty stdout. Help exits with status 0. No match is never silently assigned a new name. 
 Export configuration 
 ./bin/localproxy config export
./bin/localproxy config export --format yaml
./bin/localproxy config export -o snapshot.yaml
./bin/localproxy config export --json --output snapshot.json
./bin/localproxy config export --yaml -o - 
 config  alone is shorthand for  config export . The default is JSON on stdout.  --format json|yaml ,  --json , and  --yaml  select the format; choose one.  -o FILE  and  --output FILE  choose the destination, with  -  meaning stdout. These flags go after  config export ; global  -config  and  -file  go before  config . 
 Selection Result 
 No format or output flags JSON on stdout 
 -o snapshot.yaml  or  -o snapshot.yml YAML inferred from the filename, case-insensitively 
 -o snapshot.json , another extension, or no extension JSON 
 --format yaml -o snapshot.json Explicit YAML wins over the extension 
 --yaml -o - YAML on stdout 
 
 The export contains the complete effective registry after project-map merging: listener ports, suffix, route names and sources, Host overrides, suppressed ports, selected project file, directory backend, and the persisted tailnet setting. Routes are sorted by domain and suppressed ports numerically. Optional default fields are omitted, as in the registry schema; an empty route list is  [] . 
 Export reads configuration without contacting Caddy, probing apps or Tailscale, or writing runtime state. It does not prove that Caddy has applied the configuration. JSON can be read again with  -config ; YAML has matching field names for other tools, but  -config  still accepts only JSON. This full configuration is different from a flat  proxy.yaml  project map. The selected  project_file  path is retained; transferring the export to another machine also requires handling that dependency. 
 File output leaves stdout empty, replaces regular files atomically, preserves existing permissions, and creates new files with mode  0600 . Parent directories must exist. Export refuses to overwrite the input registry or selected project map, including file aliases, and rejects symlink or nonregular destinations. Invalid configuration or options leave existing output untouched; errors go to stderr and exit nonzero. 
 ./bin/localproxy -config /path/to/routes.json -file /path/to/proxy.yaml \
  config export --format yaml --output snapshot.yaml
./bin/localproxy config export --yaml > snapshot.yaml 
 With shell redirection, the shell truncates the destination before the CLI runs. Use  --output  when replacing a file to retain the export command's validation and atomic replacement behavior. 
 Agent instructions and skill 
 Both command groups default to  print . Output is plain Markdown on stdout, suitable for reading or piping into another tool. Printing does not read the registry, inspect project maps, contact Caddy, or write files. 
 ./bin/localproxy agents
./bin/localproxy agents print
./bin/localproxy skill print 
 Installation previews the destination and proposed content on stderr, then asks for confirmation. Answer  y  or  yes  to apply it. A negative response, blank response, or end of input makes no change. Use  --yes  only after authorizing the edit, for scripts or automation. 
 ./bin/localproxy agents install
./bin/localproxy agents install --path /path/to/project/AGENTS.md
./bin/localproxy skill install
./bin/localproxy skill install --path .agents/skills/local-proxy

# Explicit approval for a scripted installation:
./bin/localproxy agents install --path /path/to/project/AGENTS.md --yes 
 Option Meaning 
 agents install --path FILE Defaults to AGENTS.md in the current directory, or an existing lowercase agents.md when uppercase is absent. If both exist, select one explicitly. 
 skill install --path DIRECTORY Writes SKILL.md inside this directory. Defaults to $CODEX_HOME/skills/local-proxy, or ~/.codex/skills/local-proxy when CODEX_HOME is unset. 
 --yes Explicitly approve installation without prompting. The content preview still appears. 
 --help Show command-group or install usage. 
 
 The AGENTS installer appends or updates the section between  <!-- localproxy:begin -->  and  <!-- localproxy:end --> . Surrounding instructions and existing file permissions are preserved. Identical installs do nothing. Malformed or duplicate markers, symlink destinations, and edits detected during confirmation fail without replacing the file. 
 The skill installer replaces only its destination SKILL.md after confirmation and preserves other files in the skill directory. Use  $local-proxy  in a new agent session after installation. Both instruction documents are embedded in the binary, so no network or source checkout is required. Avoid redirecting printed output over existing instruction files; installation handles preservation and confirmation. 
 Editor options 
 ./bin/localproxy -config /path/to/routes.json ui \
  --listen 127.0.0.1:18083 \
  --proxy-admin 127.0.0.1:2021 \
  --proxy-config /path/to/.local/caddy.json 
 Option Default / purpose --listen 127.0.0.1:18083 . Must use a loopback IP. --proxy-admin Registry admin port on loopback. Selects the Caddy instance to update. --proxy-config Optional path to an instance-specific config snapshot to update for restarts. 
 ui --tailnet  currently has no effect. Persist the option with  reload --tailnet  or  generate --tailnet  first.  -file  is also not applied by the early UI dispatch; establish the selected map with a generating command before starting the UI. 
 Files and defaults 
 Setting Default Registry routes.json  in the current directory Suffix test HTTP / HTTPS ports 80  /  443 Caddy admin endpoint 127.0.0.1:2021 Generated JSON .local/caddy.json , alongside the registry Local CA data .local/caddy-data , alongside the registry Registry lock .local/registry.lock , alongside the registry 
 The executable lookup order is  CADDY_BIN , a  caddy  executable on PATH, then  caddy  beside the localproxy binary. The existing Go integration test specifically needs  bin/caddy . 
 Common sequences 
 ./bin/localproxy add app 3000
./bin/localproxy add api 8080
./bin/localproxy rename app studio
./bin/localproxy list
./bin/localproxy remove api 
 These commands use the current registry and can reload its running Caddy instance. Use the  isolated demo  to experiment with a disposable registry first.

title: How it works
description: Follow a request from a local name to its original localhost port.
text:
The request path 
 REQUEST ROUTING Browser → Caddy host match → App / directory DNS and TLS happen before the request can reach an application route. 
 Caddy matches each registered hostname and proxies to  127.0.0.1:<port> . A terminal fallback returns the generated static directory or proxies to the optional editor server. Both generated HTTP and HTTPS servers use this route list. 
 The Go process does not sit in the application request path. Choosing Go for this CLI helps with packaging and control operations; app proxy throughput is governed by Caddy, the upstream, and the surrounding system. No benchmark here establishes a Go-versus-Rust proxy advantage. 
 The configuration path 
 Read the registry and select a project map. Merge file defaults, persisted overrides, and discovered names. Validate names, reserved labels, and port conflicts. Write generated Caddy JSON and apply it when the command calls for a reload. 
 CLI mutations use a shared file lock to serialize registry operations. Browser edits add optimistic revision checks so two users cannot silently overwrite each other’s work. Individual file replacement is atomic, but several files and a running Caddy config are not one atomic storage system. 
 Source map 
 File Responsibility main.go CLI commands, validation, registry writes, Caddy configuration project.go YAML/JSON parsing, map selection, precedence discover.go Listener parsing, HTTP probes, random names tailnet.go Tailscale status, Serve detection, direct-listener links ui.go Directory rendering, API guards, edit persistence web/directory.html Embedded app interface, editing and confirmation 
 Operational boundaries 
 The admin endpoint controls Caddy and remains on loopback. The editor is also loopback-only at its own listener. A separate directory listener can share editing access over a tailnet, but  --tailnet  alone does not create one. 
 The directory’s Host and CSRF checks protect request boundaries, not user identity. Registry state is not a health check. Project-file reads are immediate, whereas routing changes require applying the configuration. These distinctions explain several  review findings . 
 Where performance work helps 
 The embedded HTML template is parsed once and reused with per-request data. HEAD directory requests skip rendering and Tailscale subprocesses after configuration and Host validation. Editable Caddy configuration skips generating an unused static page. 
 These improvements reduce directory and configuration work.  Measured microbenchmarks  keep those results separate from app proxy throughput.

title: Verification
description: Working examples, real captures, tests, and measured performance.
text:
Verification snapshot 
 Checked on September 22, 2026, on Linux/amd64 with Go 1.27.1 and Caddy 2.11.4. The code review pins the application source to commit  4868827 . Documentation scripts and captures are stored alongside these pages. 
 Evidence What it verifies 19 example checks Real Caddy, HTTP, strict HTTPS with .dev.test, project files, edits, conflicts, and teardown Go race tests + vet Application suite, including real Caddy integration when bin/caddy exists Four browser captures Real directory, inline editor, confirmation, and mobile layout Site browser checks Navigation, search, copy, images, mobile layout, and browser errors Code review Four reproduced limitations and their documentation consequences 
 Read the example run’s JSON evidence ,  the exact quickstart checks ,  the site browser report ,  review the findings , or  inspect screenshot provenance . A passing fixture does not establish system DNS, browser trust, or access from another tailnet device. 
 Rerun working examples 
 go build -o bin/localproxy .
python3 scripts/verify-docs-example.py \
  --output .local/docs-evidence/examples.json 
 The helper starts temporary app and Caddy processes on available high loopback ports. It verifies both certificate-chain and hostname checks using the generated CA and suffix  dev.test . It checks that successful edits change running routes and that a stale revision is rejected. Its final check confirms process and temporary-directory cleanup. 
 Run the application suite 
 go test -race -count=1 ./...
go vet ./... 
 Put Caddy at  bin/caddy  to run the existing real-proxy integration test. Without it, that test skips even if Caddy exists elsewhere on PATH. The suite checks HTTP routing, Go-verified HTTPS, unknown-name fallback, upstream 404s, map precedence, conflicting edits, malformed requests, rollback, and custom listener preservation. 
 Reproduce the screenshots 
 The PNGs are captures of the actual application, not mockups. Capture uses default  .test  over HTTP with two fixture apps and no tailnet links. Port numbers vary. The helper opens an edit confirmation and cancels; it asserts no write requests and unchanged fixture files. 
 npm install --prefix .cache/browser-test --no-save playwright-core
python3 scripts/docs-demo.py --state-file .local/docs-capture-state.json 
 In a second terminal: 
 CHROMIUM_BIN=/usr/bin/chromium \
  node scripts/capture-docs.cjs --state .local/docs-capture-state.json 
 Stop the demo with Ctrl+C afterwards. See  the capture guide  for environment overrides and alternate output locations. 
 Build and check this site 
 The  captioned demo recording  shows search, editing, a confirmed rename, and Undo in a disposable fixture. Its capture helper checks the changed and restored domains through real Caddy requests. MP4 and WebM playback and caption loading are checked in the docs browser verifier. See  media provenance and reproduction . 
 python3 scripts/build-docs.py
python3 scripts/serve-docs.py --port 18084
# In another terminal:
node scripts/verify-docs-site.cjs --url http://127.0.0.1:18084/ 
 The builder uses only Python’s standard library and emits static files to  .local/docs-site . It validates local HTML links, anchors, and duplicate IDs. The browser check additionally requires Chromium and playwright-core. The static artifact uses relative URLs and can be hosted under a repository subpath. 
 Performance measurements 
 The previous performance pass measured medians of three 300 ms runs on an Intel i9-13900HK with  GOMAXPROCS=4 , 10 routes, a warm file cache, and tailnet detection disabled. 
 Operation Before → after Measured change Directory GET handler 337.4 → 125.4 µs 2.69× faster Directory HEAD handler 321.4 → 12.4 µs 25.99× faster Editable config generation 361.9 → 59.6 µs 6.07× faster 
 These are Go microbenchmarks of control operations, not browser load times or application proxy throughput. No performance benchmark was rerun just to build these docs. Read  the complete methodology and results . 
 GOMAXPROCS=4 go test -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(Directory|CaddyConfig)' \
  -benchmem -benchtime=300ms -count=3

title: Code review
description: An independent review of the current implementation and its failure modes.
text:
Review scope 
 An independent sub-agent reviewed the Go CLI, route merging, discovery, Caddy generation, directory API, Tailscale links, and tests. Other agents exercised runnable examples and captured the real UI. Collaboration used the available built-in agent messaging; Mayfly chat was not available in this environment. 
 The application was reviewed at  commit 4868827  on September 22, 2026. The documentation work leaves core application code unchanged.  Read the full review with source references and reproduction details . 
 Medium · Default wildcard compatibility 
 The generated  *.test  certificate is accepted by the existing Go verifier but rejected by the tested Python/OpenSSL and curl clients for  app.test . Both clients explicitly trusted the generated CA; failure was hostname matching. 
 Workaround:  configure suffix  dev.test , update existing route domains and full map keys to match, and configure matching DNS or use curl  --resolve . The isolated verifier uses this suffix and verifies TLS normally. Browser behavior was not established by these HTTP screenshots. 
 Medium · Saved and running routes can differ 
 CLI mutations write the registry and generated configuration before reloading Caddy. A failed reload returns an error but leaves the changed registry saved. When the admin endpoint is unavailable, automatic route updates skip reload. 
 Recovery:  inspect the saved config, fix the reload error, and run  reload . The CLI’s  list  command describes merged registry data, not an independently confirmed view of active routes. A future improvement would share apply-and-persist logic with the editor. 
 Medium · File edits appear before application 
 The editor merges project files on every directory request. Editing the file can therefore change visible names before the running Caddy routes change. A successful browser rename can also apply the complete currently merged set. 
 Workflow:  run  reload  after changing a project map. A future UI could distinguish pending defaults from applied routes. 
 Low · UI tailnet flag has no effect 
 The CLI accepts  ui --tailnet  but dispatches the UI before applying the global flag. An isolated reproduction returned  tailnet_enabled: false . 
 Workaround:  enable it with  reload --tailnet  for a running instance, or  generate --tailnet  before startup, then run the UI. 
 What the implementation already checks 
 Strict request parsing, bounded bodies, Host and CSRF checks, shared file locking, and revision checks cover common editing failures. Concurrent rendering tests check that tokens and URLs remain request-specific. Real Caddy tests verify routing and reload behavior, and UI tests cover explicit reload rejection and persistence rollback. 
 Remaining useful work includes regression tests for these four findings, interrupted reload recovery, and remote access checks from a second tailnet device. This review is scoped engineering evidence, not a comprehensive security audit.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Check DNS, TLS, routing, and the editor one layer at a time.
text:
The domain does not resolve 
 Registering a name does not configure your resolver. Check  getent hosts app.test  or the name under your chosen suffix. It must resolve to loopback for local app routes. Use the quickstart’s  curl --resolve  command to test routing independently. Check whether browser DNS-over-HTTPS bypasses the local resolver. 
 HTTPS reports a certificate error 
 Distinguish an untrusted issuer from a hostname mismatch. Use the instance’s generated  root.crt  with  --cacert  to test trust. If the error says  app.test  does not match  *.test  in curl/Python, use the  documented .dev.test workaround . Installing the root again will not change hostname matching. 
 A registered app fails 
 Open its original  http://localhost:<port>  link. Confirm the app accepts IPv4 loopback connections and its port matches the registry. If it rejects the custom hostname, allow that hostname in the app or set the route’s  localhost_host  option and reload. App 404s and upstream failures are not replaced with the directory. 
 An unknown name gets 403 
 The editable directory restricts Host headers. Use an unregistered single-label name under your configured suffix, such as  missing.dev.test , or the machine’s recognized local/Tailscale address. Arbitrary external Host headers are rejected. Static and editable fallback have different Host behavior. 
 Editing is missing or fails 
 Check that  directory_address  is configured, the UI process is listening at that address, and Caddy has reloaded it. The static directory has no editing controls. For an instance-specific admin port, pass  --proxy-admin ; use  --proxy-config  to retain its restart snapshot. 
 Refresh after a revision conflict. If Caddy rejects a browser edit, inspect its logs before retrying. If a CLI command reports a failed reload, its registry change may already be saved; correct the failure and reload. Do not assume the directory confirms active upstream health. 
 The map or rename seems ignored 
 Overrides outrank map entries. Check  name_source  and  project_file  in the registry. If both  proxy.yaml  and  proxy.json  exist, choose one using  -file  before the command. Run CLI commands from a directory without an unrelated map, or select the intended file explicitly. File edits need a reload. 
 Tailnet links are unavailable 
 Enable the saved setting with  reload --tailnet , rather than  ui --tailnet . Check  tailscale status  and whether the app already has a suitable listener or Serve endpoint. A localhost-only app cannot be reached at the machine’s Tailscale IP just because a link is displayed. Check access rules and firewalls from the other device. 
 Startup says a port is in use 
 Inspect  ss -ltnp . Give each instance distinct HTTP, HTTPS, admin, and UI ports; keep app ports separate from these. Use high ports for an unprivileged test. The  demo script  chooses available ports and avoids your normal registry. 
 The docs preview is not running 
 python3 scripts/build-docs.py
python3 scripts/serve-docs.py --port 18084 
 Open  http://127.0.0.1:18084 . Search loads a local JSON file, so serve the site over HTTP rather than opening HTML directly from disk. No backend API, CDN, font service, or external JavaScript is needed.
